note: Indicators on watch: the measurable dials this narrative argues through. Extracted from the corpus transcripts (every threshold is attributed to the speaker who named it in a video; nothing here is a Narrative Radar forecast).
method: transcript extraction (31 transcripts, 312 indicator mentions) + editorial synthesis + adversarial fabrication/misattribution check (2 corrections applied)

indicators.name: AI capex vs AI revenue
indicators.punchline: The whole 2026 thesis in two numbers: roughly $700 billion a year pouring into AI against about $110 billion coming back out.

thresholds.level: $700B+ of AI buildout spending this year vs ~$110B of AI revenue — about 2.5 cents of every dollar of US GDP
thresholds.meaning: Leg one of the four-leg parlay: revenue has to multiply, not just grow, for the bet to pay

thresholds.level: $725 billion of hyperscaler capex in 2026, up 77% year over year
thresholds.meaning: The buildout as a cheap-credit malinvestment cluster — the modern skyscraper curse
thresholds.predictor: David Lin (headline), analyzed by Mark Thornton

thresholds.level: $2.4 trillion spent vs $50 billion of profit — a $2.35 trillion collective loss
thresholds.meaning: By basic math the bubble has already burst

thresholds.level: AI firms' revenue about one-tenth of costs
thresholds.meaning: AI is overinvested ~10x sustainable scale; the bust alone causes a US recession within one or two years

thresholds.level: $1.57 of capex per $1 of cash flow back ($534B capex through 2027 vs $340B cash-flow growth)
thresholds.meaning: Only works if AI growth keeps scaling into these valuations

thresholds.level: Capex now 94 cents of every dollar of operating cash flow, up from 40-50 cents (PIMCO)
thresholds.meaning: The buildout is draining the vault instead of the vault funding the buildout

thresholds.level: Return on each incremental cloud dollar sliding from ~40% toward 20%, projections pointing to 10%
thresholds.meaning: Leg two: the shrinkage has to stop for the parlay to hit

thresholds.level: AI capex = 49.5% of Q1 2026 GDP growth; Alphabet's first negative free cash flow since its 2004 listing after $45B of quarterly capex
thresholds.meaning: Any slowdown risks negative GDP, layoffs and a big market correction

thresholds.level: $2.9 trillion buildout through 2028 against $1.4 trillion of cash flow — a $1.5 trillion hole (Morgan Stanley)
thresholds.meaning: Leg three: the borrowing window has to stay open

thresholds.level: OpenAI at a $1 trillion valuation on $13 billion of revenue against $26 billion of expenses; 95% of generative-AI pilots fail; only ~2% of US households pay for AI
thresholds.meaning: Valuations detached from any paying demand
thresholds.predictor: Casey Simpson (OpenAI figures, 95% pilot failure); household figure unattributed

indicators.contested_note: Identical spending, opposite verdicts: Simpson and Keen read the revenue gap as proof the bubble has already burst, while Google Cloud's 82% growth and $514 billion backlog — plus Anthropic at ~$70B and OpenAI at ~$37B annualized revenue — are cited as evidence the demand is real.

indicators.name: Off-balance-sheet AI debt and circular financing
indicators.punchline: Five tech companies owe $1.65 trillion that never appears on a balance sheet — more than all the debt they actually admit to.

thresholds.level: $1.65 trillion off-balance-sheet vs about $1.35 trillion on the books across the big five (Nikkei Research puts it near $1.7 trillion)
thresholds.meaning: Leverage is far higher than balance sheets suggest — why some compare this to 2008 and Enron rather than 2000

thresholds.level: Nearly $1 trillion of pledged data-center leases with over $660 billion invisible; roughly $1.8 trillion industry-wide (Moody's / Morgan Stanley)
thresholds.meaning: The same bet written five times, funded by the same small club of lenders

thresholds.level: Hyperscaler bond issuance: $28B/year average 2020-24, over $100B in 2025, $159B in the first five months of 2026
thresholds.meaning: More borrowed in five months than in the previous five years combined

thresholds.level: Tech now nearly 18% of all US investment-grade debt outstanding
thresholds.meaning: Concentration the IMF is flagging as a financial-stability worry

thresholds.level: Meta's Hyperion SPV: $27.3 billion of bonds running to 2049 against a lease starting 2029 in four-year chunks; Meta owns 20% but guarantees up to ~$28 billion
thresholds.meaning: 24-year debt resting on a four-year commitment — the structure tells two different stories

thresholds.level: Alphabet raised $32 billion across four currencies in under 24 hours; the 100-year bond roughly 10x oversubscribed
thresholds.meaning: The deepest capital market on earth is being tested by what these firms need to borrow

thresholds.level: CoreWeave forced above 10% on bonds; Google raising $25B of bonds plus a planned $40B share sale
thresholds.meaning: Rising funding costs are the specific mechanism that pops the AI capex cycle

thresholds.level: Nvidia committing up to $100 billion to OpenAI, which borrows against that guarantee to buy Nvidia chips
thresholds.meaning: Record chip demand partly manufactured by the seller; compute contracts booked as backlog are economically loans

thresholds.level: Off-book obligations up roughly eightfold since 2022, $120B+ moved in under two years; long-dated hyperscaler bonds trading at junk-like spreads despite top ratings
thresholds.meaning: Standardizing as fast as telecom vendor financing (1998-2000) and mortgage securitization (2004-07); lenders getting cold feet

thresholds.level: SoftBank's record domestic bond coupons — 'the week those coupons stop rising, breathe'
thresholds.meaning: The thermometer of the era: when the money behind the bubble gets expensive, a clock starts

indicators.contested_note: On the surface these are the least indebted companies in America — net debt of 0.04 times earnings, the lowest of any US sector — which is exactly the fact the bears use to argue the leverage simply moved off the books.

indicators.name: US federal debt, deficits and interest expense
indicators.punchline: $40 trillion owed, $2 trillion more borrowed every year, and interest is now the second-biggest line in the federal budget.

thresholds.level: $40 trillion national debt with $2 trillion annual deficits
thresholds.meaning: Debt plus accruing interest has backed the government into wartime-style desperation that ends in financial repression
thresholds.predictor: Mark Thornton; cited as 'approaching $40 trillion' by Willem Middelkoop and Tom Bilyeu

thresholds.level: Spends about $7 trillion against about $5 trillion of revenue — 40% more than it takes in; debt about six times income
thresholds.meaning: The level that throughout history produces problems and money-printing devaluation

thresholds.level: Over 130% debt-to-GDP sustained for roughly 18 months
thresholds.meaning: Historically ends in internal strife and an economic reset
thresholds.predictor: Tom Bilyeu citing Ray Dalio — flatly rejected by Steve Keen

thresholds.level: GAO projections: 106% of GDP by 2029, 250% in 30 years, debt growing twice as fast as the economy
thresholds.meaning: The official alarm — which Keen quotes only to call it 'completely wrong'

thresholds.level: Federal interest payments at 3.2% of GDP, back to the early-1990s record, projected to triple over 30 years
thresholds.meaning: Debt service starts squeezing out everything else the government does
thresholds.predictor: Steve Keen (citing GAO); Tom Bilyeu calls interest the second-biggest budget line item

thresholds.level: Budget deficit 5.8% of GDP against the administration's 3% target
thresholds.meaning: The 3-3-3 agenda missed on every leg — growth 1.9% vs 3%, oil +0.57M barrels/day vs 3M

thresholds.level: The point at which new debt can no longer be sold to pay off the old
thresholds.meaning: The Ponzi threshold — governments default when the queue for the next tranche ends

thresholds.level: Six new UK prime ministers in seven years
thresholds.meaning: The political symptom of a government that has run out of money — the late-cycle cautionary tale

indicators.contested_note: Steve Keen calls this the wrong debt entirely — a currency-issuing government creates the money, and deficits are the band-aid (20% of GDP in COVID versus the New Deal's 5% peak) that stops private-debt busts from becoming depressions.

indicators.name: Long-term Treasury yields and the Fed's next move
indicators.punchline: The narrative's favorite tripwire: the 30-year Treasury above 5% for 27 straight sessions, with a possible rate hike landing September 16.

thresholds.level: 30-year Treasury above 5% — 27 straight sessions, currently 5.2%
thresholds.meaning: Danger level for the economy, and the Fed is trapped: cutting short rates would push long rates higher still

thresholds.level: 30-year closing at 5.27 after the July meeting — a 20-to-22-year high
thresholds.meaning: Echoes the multi-year Treasury highs seen at the dot-com top; raises funding costs economy-wide

thresholds.level: US 10-year around 4.7%, close to all-time highs
thresholds.meaning: Rising partly because Japan, the most reliable foreign buyer, is stepping back — it sets mortgages and corporate borrowing

thresholds.level: A hike at the September 16 meeting; three hikes (September, October, December) per Bank of America; 80,000 jobs the swing print
thresholds.meaning: The same move that popped the dot-com bubble, arriving exactly 38 months after the last hike — the same gap as the May 2000 'nail in the coffin' hike

thresholds.level: Dot-com analog: six hikes from 4.75% to 6.5%, market topped about 9 months after the first hike, Nasdaq 100 fell 78%
thresholds.meaning: The template now laid over the AI bubble

thresholds.level: A 25 basis point hike now
thresholds.meaning: Delay could force more aggressive tightening if inflation becomes entrenched

thresholds.level: Real (inflation-adjusted) rates near zero
thresholds.meaning: What fuelled the end-stage blow-off top of the long stock bubble

thresholds.level: QE restarted at $40 billion a month; $2.5 trillion drained out of Fed repo holdings back into the economy
thresholds.meaning: Liquidity aimed at private equity and private credit, with yield-curve control the next escalation

thresholds.level: More than $8 billion of fresh Fed liquidity in a single week
thresholds.meaning: Named as the direct reason the S&P 500 just made a new all-time high

indicators.contested_note: The same rate desk cuts both ways: Paffrath and Kashkari watch for the hike that pops the bubble, while Bera Finance and J Bravo argue the Fed's liquidity injections and heavy T-bill issuance are exactly what keeps producing new highs.

indicators.name: Margin debt and retail leverage
indicators.punchline: A record $1.5 trillion is borrowed against stocks — up almost 150% since Q4 2023, a level seen only in 2000, 2007 and 2021.

thresholds.level: FINRA margin debt approximately $1.5 trillion in June — a record
thresholds.meaning: Extra buying power on the way up, brutal forced selling when prices fall

thresholds.level: Margin debt up almost 150% since Q4 2023, to levels only seen at the 2000, 2007 and 2021 tops
thresholds.meaning: Proof the rally is speculation and hype rather than fundamentals

thresholds.level: Margin debt about 4% of GDP now versus 9% of GDP at the 1929 peak; 0.8 correlation with the CAPE over 100 years of data
thresholds.meaning: Change in margin debt is what drives the valuation itself

thresholds.level: US margin investing at 4.7% of the market versus Korea's 1.3% peak and the 2% before the dot-com bust
thresholds.meaning: An AI crash here would hit far harder than Korea's did

thresholds.level: 13.8 trillion won in 2x single-stock leveraged ETFs behind a KOSPI that ran up 265-272% then fell 38-44% (~$2 trillion wiped out, 1.2 million leveraged households)
thresholds.meaning: The margin-call doom loop demonstrated live — and the same products are growing popular in the US
thresholds.predictor: JJ (John Johnston) (265% run-up, 38% fall); Casey Simpson (272%, ~40% fall, 1.2M leveraged households); Ed Elson (ProfG Markets) (44%, $2T wiped out); Graham Stephan (13.8T won of 2x single-stock leveraged ETFs)

thresholds.level: A roughly 4x-levered AI fund peaking at $20-40 billion, unwound within July
thresholds.meaning: The first domino of forced deleveraging tied to the Korea crash

thresholds.level: Half a dozen significant forced-selling events in the month of August
thresholds.meaning: A dated countdown for leveraged AI holders to watch unfold

thresholds.level: Call option volume at the highest level ever; collateral requirements recently loosened
thresholds.meaning: Retail all-in with borrowed money — the classic 'weak hands' sign
thresholds.predictor: J Bravo (options); Cenk Uygur (collateral rules); Ray Dalio (weak hands / leveraged ETFs)

indicators.contested_note: Bulls read the same leverage as depth of demand — over $400 billion of announced buybacks, up 20% year over year, plus automatic 401(k) inflows — while bears see only fuel for the Korean margin-call spiral.

indicators.name: Gold, silver and the dollar's reserve share
indicators.punchline: Central banks have bought roughly 1,000 tonnes of gold a year for five years running — about a third of everything mined.

thresholds.level: 5% to 15% of any portfolio in gold / hard money
thresholds.meaning: Gold does best precisely when stocks, bonds and cash do worst; it is still the second-largest central-bank reserve currency

thresholds.level: Roughly 1,000 tonnes of central-bank buying annually for five consecutive years — about one-third of global mine production
thresholds.meaning: Governments preparing for a less dollar-dominant monetary system

thresholds.level: Gold's share of reserves toward 30% now versus 40%+ historically; a return to that share implies $12,000-$14,000 an ounce
thresholds.meaning: The sovereign-debt-crisis price target, now discussed by major banks rather than only gold advocates
thresholds.predictor: Willem Middelkoop / narrator citing a major bank

thresholds.level: $7,000-$8,000 gold with a shot at $11,000 by 2032
thresholds.meaning: Priced off the sovereign-debt and political-crisis timeline

thresholds.level: Metals declining at least into August, possibly into early 2027, then a bull market running from 2027 into 2032
thresholds.meaning: A dated cycle call that contradicts the buy-now urgency elsewhere in the corpus

thresholds.level: Silver $100 in coming months, with the bull market ending near $500 on a gold-to-silver ratio moving toward 10-to-1
thresholds.meaning: The leveraged version of the same trade in a small physical market

thresholds.level: Gold pulled back from nearly $5,500 and may briefly dip below $4,000
thresholds.meaning: Framed as profit-taking, not a new bear market, while central banks keep buying

thresholds.level: Dollar still about 56.8% of global official FX reserves (Q4 2025), roughly 55% of international banking claims and 60% of liabilities
thresholds.meaning: Gradual decline, not collapse — the one video that checks the IMF data concludes no sudden dollar collapse is happening

thresholds.level: About 1% of my portfolio in Bitcoin
thresholds.meaning: Unprintable money, but quantum, surveillance and tax risks make gold the preferred hard money

indicators.contested_note: Same reserve data, opposite stories: Dalio and Middelkoop read central-bank gold buying as the dollar order ending, while the corpus's one data-checking video finds the dollar still at 56.8% of reserves and concludes no collapse is under way — and Armstrong argues capital fleeing war flows into the US, which is why the dollar falls last.

indicators.name: Valuation gauges (Shiller CAPE, Buffett indicator, forward P/E)
indicators.punchline: CAPE is sitting at 41 — the dot-com peak was 44 — on a market worth about 2.3 times the entire US economy.

thresholds.level: Shiller CAPE at 41, almost matching the dot-com peak of 44
thresholds.meaning: One of the most expensive stock markets in history

thresholds.level: CAPE crossing the 40 threshold; today right around 41
thresholds.meaning: Corroborates that the market is overwhelmingly expensive

thresholds.level: CAPE almost 40 versus a 17.9 long-term average — matched only by December 1999 (then -50%) and approached in 1929 (P/E 33, then a 70-80% drop)
thresholds.meaning: Either prices fall or earnings rise; there is no third option

thresholds.level: CAPE about 40 versus a historical average of 14 to 16
thresholds.meaning: A ridiculous bubble, driven by margin debt

thresholds.level: Buffett indicator at 219 — more than two standard deviations above trend
thresholds.meaning: Near-record expensiveness confirmed by a second, independent gauge

thresholds.level: Buffett indicator around 230%, past the 200% 'playing with fire' line
thresholds.meaning: Above both the 2021 and dot-com peaks — though it forecasts low 10-year returns, not crash timing
thresholds.predictor: Warren Buffett's 2001 essay, quoted by the narrator

thresholds.level: Forward P/E 20.7 versus a 10-year average of 19; a 5% earnings miss plus compression to 16 equals a 25% S&P drop
thresholds.meaning: A big fall that requires no recession at all

thresholds.level: Expected 10-year stock return of zero or negative on a 10-year moving average
thresholds.meaning: Bonds and real estate offer the same zero-to-negative real returns

thresholds.level: The AI bubble sized at 17 times the dot-com bubble and 4 times the 2008 mortgage crisis
thresholds.meaning: Bursting would destroy the world economy

indicators.contested_note: Two caveats travel with every one of these numbers — corporate margins are structurally higher (about 12% of GDP versus 7-8% historically) and Stephan calls a 20.7 forward P/E 'not crazy' — so even the bears' own gauges say expensive, not timed.

indicators.name: Index concentration in the AI megacaps
indicators.punchline: Seven companies are almost 40% of the S&P 500 — the index fund in your 401(k) is one trade wearing a diversification costume.

thresholds.level: Magnificent Seven at more than a third, almost 40% of the S&P 500
thresholds.meaning: If they fall, the entire market and everyone's index funds fall with them

thresholds.level: Largest 10 stocks roughly 37% of the index — a 25% fall in those names alone is a 9% index drop before any panic selling
thresholds.meaning: Historically dangerous, though less extreme than Korea

thresholds.level: Mega-caps at around 41% of the entire S&P 500
thresholds.meaning: A handful of names drag the whole index's valuation to record levels

thresholds.level: Samsung and SK Hynix were more than half of Korea's entire index
thresholds.meaning: A diversified index turned into a single bet on memory chips — then it crashed

thresholds.level: Seven US companies account for 90% of AI capex; the top five over 80%
thresholds.meaning: The boom rests on a handful of spending decisions by a handful of executives

thresholds.level: Index-versus-breadth divergence not seen since the year 2000
thresholds.meaning: The S&P moving opposite most of its own stocks is usually a sign something is wrong

indicators.contested_note: Bulls point at breadth as the rebuttal — small caps up 16% and the equal-weight S&P at record highs suggest the rally is broadening beyond the seven names rather than narrowing into them.

indicators.name: Inflation rate and the cumulative price level
indicators.punchline: Prices are about 30% higher than before COVID and never came back down; at 3.5-4% a year, holding cash is a slow guaranteed loss.

thresholds.level: Inflation at about 3.5% or 4% a year, roughly where it is now
thresholds.meaning: Makes cash nearly guaranteed to be the worst long-term investment despite feeling safest

thresholds.level: About 30% cumulative inflation over the last six years
thresholds.meaning: COVID money printing into a supply-constrained economy, never reversed — it impoverished the bottom of the K-shaped economy

thresholds.level: Consumer prices running 4 to 4.5% against the Fed's 2% target
thresholds.meaning: The Fed reaches 2% only by redefining the statistics; food and energy lead prices higher

thresholds.level: 'The only thing with a three in front of it is inflation'
thresholds.meaning: The administration's 3-3-3 growth/deficit/oil agenda missed on every leg except the unwanted one

indicators.contested_note: Keen puts the price spike on private lending and constrained supply — 92% of US money creation from 2000-2024 was private, only 8% government — so for him inflation indicts the banks, not the deficit Bilyeu and Dalio blame.

indicators.name: The 80-year big cycle and its dated deadlines
indicators.punchline: The genre's master clock: an 80-year order that last reset in 1945, and a computer model that puts the end of this one at 2032.

thresholds.level: Roughly 80 years per big cycle, last reset in 1945; the US and UK are 'later in that cycle'
thresholds.meaning: The monetary, domestic-political and geopolitical orders break down together at the end

thresholds.level: About six years, give or take three, from one recession to the next
thresholds.meaning: The short business cycle nested inside the big one, driven by loosening and tightening

thresholds.level: 2032 — the collapse of republican forms of government
thresholds.meaning: The terminal date from Armstrong's computer model, after which a new political system emerges

thresholds.level: Global recession intensifying after 2026 and probably bottoming around 2028; China taking Taiwan at least by 2027
thresholds.meaning: 1970s-style stagflation with cost-push inflation that rate hikes cannot cure

thresholds.level: Between the midterm elections and the 2028 presidential election
thresholds.meaning: The window in which political and social conflict intensifies toward possibly irreconcilable differences

thresholds.level: Late-cycle policy markers: wealth taxes (a 2% levy on net worth over 10 million discussed in the UK), capital controls, exit taxes, debt restructuring
thresholds.meaning: The historical playbook when governments run out of money — and the forced selling that pricks the bubble

indicators.contested_note: Dalio undercuts his own clock — judge a country by measurable condition, like a physical exam, not by elapsed years — while Armstrong's 2032 is a fixed date from a model, which is how the same 'cycle' supports both 'any moment now' and 'seven years away'.

indicators.name: The yen, JGB yields and the carry trade
indicators.punchline: One line the whole world is watching: 164 yen to the dollar, the level banks treat as Japan's breaking point.

thresholds.level: USD/JPY 164 — JP Morgan's 'magic line in the sand', with the yen near 160, its weakest in about 40 years
thresholds.meaning: Watch-item one: the level Japan supposedly will not let it cross

thresholds.level: Japanese government debt over 200% of GDP — more than Greece at collapse
thresholds.meaning: Every percentage point of higher rates becomes a huge interest bill once the bond market wakes up
thresholds.predictor: Andrei Jikh; Meerkat; Martin Armstrong calls it the highest of any major country

thresholds.level: Bank of Japan holds about 48% of all JGBs; foreigners under 8%
thresholds.meaning: The arrangement that let Japan survive its debt — now being dismantled in real time

thresholds.level: 10-year JGB about 2.7%, ten times higher than 2022's 0.25%; 30-year around 4%
thresholds.meaning: The sleeping bond market has woken up after 30 years

thresholds.level: Japan CPI at 1.6%, below the BOJ's 2% goal for a fifth straight month, while yields still rise
thresholds.meaning: JGBs now trade on who will buy the debt, not on inflation — proof the machine is broken

thresholds.level: $73 billion of yen buying bought only three weeks; reserves for about 15 more interventions of that size; a hike to 1% failed too
thresholds.meaning: Japan cannot defend its currency by buying it, which forces the repatriation plan

thresholds.level: Hedge funds net short around 150,000 yen contracts (~$11-12 billion)
thresholds.meaning: Billions betting Japan is helpless — described as the tip of the iceberg

thresholds.level: Crypto tax cut from 55% to 20% for repatriated wealth with JGB-backed stablecoins; insurers' biggest JGB buying in three years, funded by selling US Treasuries
thresholds.meaning: Japan manufacturing a new buyer for its own debt — and making repatriation an American problem

indicators.contested_note: Bilyeu raises the yen carry unwind as a live global danger while Keen dismisses it outright as long as Japan runs a trade surplus — and Jikh's own twist is that a stronger yen this time is Tokyo's deliberate plan, not the crisis signal it was in 1998, 2008 and August 2024.

indicators.name: Insider selling and smart-money cash piles
indicators.punchline: Insiders are selling at the fastest pace in recorded history while Berkshire sits on nearly $400 billion of cash.

thresholds.level: Berkshire's record cash nearing $400 billion, a net seller for 12+ quarters totalling over $150 billion
thresholds.meaning: Nothing is worth buying at these prices — sitting out, not calling a crash

thresholds.level: US insiders selling at the fastest rate in recorded history, buying at half the normal rate
thresholds.meaning: Not a smoking gun, but not a vote of confidence at record valuations

thresholds.level: Bezos's $4 billion Amazon sale — his last comparable sale was May 2021, after which Amazon fell about 50%
thresholds.meaning: Insider selling as a cycle-top signal

thresholds.level: Micron's CEO selling $37 million of stock; Norway's $2.2 trillion sovereign fund pulling back from Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple and Google
thresholds.meaning: The first blips of institutional flight from the AI trade

thresholds.level: Fund managers holding only about 3.6% cash — 96% invested
thresholds.meaning: Positioning is maxed out, nobody is hedged, and there is little left to buy the dip with

thresholds.level: Insider sales and surging stock issuance increase the supply of stock
thresholds.meaning: Rising supply plus a need for cash is part of the mechanism that pops a bubble

indicators.contested_note: Stephan is explicit that this is 'not a smoking gun' and J Bravo relays Burry's 1987-style warning with open sarcasm — the same selling reads as smart money exiting or as rich people simply rebalancing.

indicators.name: AI job displacement and the labour share
indicators.punchline: A Senate committee report puts nearly 100 million American jobs at risk within a decade — and 70% of Americans already expect fewer jobs.

thresholds.level: Nearly 100 million US jobs replaceable over the next decade — 47% of truck drivers, 64% of accountants, 89% of fast-food workers
thresholds.meaning: The core evidence for reining in the AI race

thresholds.level: Most white-collar work fully automated within the next 12 to 18 months
thresholds.meaning: Industry leaders forecasting imminent automation in their own words
thresholds.predictor: Mustafa Suleyman, quoted by Bernie Sanders

thresholds.level: 30,000 layoffs each at Amazon and Oracle, 20,000 at Microsoft, 18,000 at Meta; AI-native firms running with about 25% fewer employees
thresholds.meaning: The jobs impact is already underway, not theoretical

thresholds.level: Big Tech fired around 1 million people expecting AI to replace them and has hired about 90% of those jobs back
thresholds.meaning: The labour-replacement thesis failed in practice

thresholds.level: The top 10% of households hold almost 90% of the stock
thresholds.meaning: AI-driven equity gains widen the wealth gap before a single job is lost
thresholds.predictor: Steven Bartlett (in the Dalio interview); echoed by TYT's Jen

thresholds.level: The labour share of business revenue falling while the owners' share rises
thresholds.meaning: AI widens the wealth gap that fuels the internal-conflict leg of the big cycle; college graduates already struggle to get hired

thresholds.level: Unemployment spikes come mainly from the bubble bursting and the ensuing debt crisis
thresholds.meaning: Dalio's own correction: the crash, not gradual AI displacement, is what creates the jobless shock

indicators.contested_note: Sanders' 100 million jobs and Suleyman's 12-to-18-month timeline sit directly against Simpson's 90% rehire rate and reports that around 90% of firms see no employment or productivity impact at all — the same technology read as a jobs apocalypse and as a failed promise.

indicators.name: Private debt and the change in credit
indicators.punchline: The one chart the doom videos skip: private credit swinging from +15% of GDP in 2006 to -5% in 2009 is what actually broke 2008.

thresholds.level: Credit (annual change in private debt) swinging from plus 15% of GDP in 2006 to minus 5% in 2009
thresholds.meaning: The swing in credit, not the level of government debt, caused the collapse — and is what let Keen call the GFC in advance

thresholds.level: Correlation of minus 0.93 between credit and unemployment (1990-2015)
thresholds.meaning: Credit and jobs are near-perfect mirror images; falling private debt shows up directly as job losses

thresholds.level: 92% of US money creation was private versus 8% government (2000-2024); 140% private in 1980-2000
thresholds.meaning: Money creation is a private-lending phenomenon, so public deficits are not the danger

thresholds.level: When bank lending goes negative, GDP falls (velocity of money stable around 1.8, usually 1.8-2.2)
thresholds.meaning: The mechanical link from credit creation and destruction straight to output

thresholds.level: COVID deficit of 20% of GDP versus the New Deal's 5% peak
thresholds.meaning: Government deficits are the band-aid that stops private-debt collapses from becoming depressions

thresholds.level: A large trade deficit forcing borrowing in foreign currency
thresholds.meaning: Keen's actual danger sign for a country — which is why he sees no crisis in surplus-running Japan

indicators.contested_note: Keen and Bilyeu agree a private-credit bust is coming and disagree completely about the culprit: Bilyeu's $2 trillion deficits and 130% debt-to-GDP against Keen's verdict that government debt is the band-aid, not the wound — the sharpest single split in the corpus.
